title: If your short videos lose people in three seconds, start with the cut
markdown:
# If your short videos lose people in three seconds, start with the cut

You post a useful 42-second video. The opening says, "Today I want to talk about a mistake I see a lot." It is polite, clear, and almost built to be swiped away.

The problem is not that viewers have no attention span. They have a thumb and a feed full of unfinished promises. In the first few seconds, they are deciding whether this clip has anything to do with them and whether staying will pay off. A broad introduction answers neither question.

The fix is smaller than a dramatic new filming style: begin with the moment of friction, then earn the explanation.

## Give the viewer something to recognize

The strongest opening usually names an experience the viewer already has. It does not need to be clever. It needs to be specific enough that the right person thinks, "Yes, that is happening to me."

Compare these two openings for a video about weak hooks:

> "Here are three tips for making better short-form videos."

> "If your videos get watched but never reach the second sentence, your opening is probably doing too much explaining."

The second line creates a useful bit of pressure. It identifies a symptom, narrows the audience, and suggests there is a reason for the symptom. It also gives the rest of the video a job: prove the diagnosis and show the repair.

Before writing a hook, write the viewer's private sentence. For example:

- "I keep starting with context because I do not know what else to say."
- "People watch the first second, then disappear."
- "My advice is good, but it sounds like everyone else's advice."

That sentence is raw material, not copy. Turn it into a line someone would stop for. Keep the language they would use, especially the annoying little detail they complain about.

## Start in the middle of the problem

Creators often begin at the beginning: a greeting, a topic label, a promise to explain. That is logical for a presentation. A feed is not a presentation. The viewer arrived halfway through a scroll, not in a seat waiting for the agenda.

Start where the tension already exists.

For a budgeting video, do not open with "How to save more money." Try: "The subscription you forgot about is not the one draining your account." The line creates a question that the next few seconds can answer.

For a fitness video, do not say "Three mistakes beginners make at the gym." Try: "Your first gym session gets harder when you copy the workout of the person who has been there for six years." It gives the beginner a recognizable scene and a reason to listen.

For a creator video, do not announce "How to improve retention." Try: "The sentence you use to sound professional may be the sentence that makes people leave." That is a claim with consequences. Now the video has somewhere to go.

The opening does not have to reveal everything. It should make one clear promise: this clip will resolve a problem, expose a mistake, or show a result the viewer cares about. If it promises five things at once, it becomes foggy again.

## Use a hook that your video can actually pay off

A hook can win a pause and still lose the viewer ten seconds later. This happens when the opening makes a giant claim, then the body gives a familiar answer. The viewer feels the mismatch even if they cannot name it.

Match the size of the hook to the evidence in the video. If you open with a contrarian claim, show the example that supports it. If you open with a question, answer it early. If you open with a before-and-after result, explain the change that produced it.

A quick test helps: remove the hook and read the next two lines. Do they feel like a direct continuation? If they do not, the hook belongs to a different video.

This is also why vague urgency wears out fast. "You need to hear this" asks for trust before it offers anything. "Your tutorial loses people before the demo starts" gives the viewer a concrete reason to stay.

## Write five openings before you film one

Do not wait for the perfect first sentence with a camera on. Write several versions while the stakes are low, then choose the one that creates the cleanest question.

Use these prompts for the same video idea:

- Name the costly mistake: "You are losing viewers before your point begins."
- Name the moment of recognition: "You can see the swipe happen right after this phrase."
- State the unpopular correction: "More energy will not fix a weak opening."
- Lead with the outcome: "This one rewrite gave the rest of the video a chance."
- Open on a scene: "At 9:14, I watched a useful video bury its best line under a greeting."

Read them aloud. The right choice is rarely the most dramatic sentence. It is the one that makes the next sentence feel inevitable.

Then film the hook twice: once as written and once a little plainer. The polished version may sound better in your notes; the plain version often sounds more like a person noticing something in real time. Keep the take that reaches the point sooner.

## A simple revision pass before you post

Watch the first ten seconds with the sound off. Can someone tell what problem the clip is about from the first visual and your opening words? Then watch it with sound on and listen for the delay before the useful part.

Cut greetings, self-introductions, and scene-setting that the viewer does not need. Keep context only when it changes the meaning of what follows. If your hook needs a long disclaimer to be true, shrink the claim.

Finally, ask one blunt question: would the person who needs this advice know, in three seconds, that it is for them? If the answer is maybe, rewrite the first line before you change the lighting, the captions, or the posting time.

Hook writing is not a trick for forcing attention. It is a way to respect the viewer's decision. Say what is at stake. Make the promise specific. Then deliver the useful part without making them wait for it.

If you want a structured way to generate and test stronger openings, try [Hook Lab](https://capafy.ai/agent/8123079349?ct=hooklab_blog).
